dimensions.name: Protocol & data-shape orientation

evidence.note: Inspected one config and dataset for every one of the six task types, confirming exact row/field schemas (queries/corpus/qrels for retrieval, test.jsonl for others) before implementing — meets the level-5 'representative inspection of each type' bar.
Printed ALL 37 task configs in one pass plus checked GPU/packages, a systematic survey across types that begins to reach the level-8 'catalogues where configs override defaults' behavior.
Follow-up verification of sklearn availability, classification train.jsonl usage, and retrieval corpus/qrels field names — targeted schema confirmation rather than assumption.

Wrote/rewrote evaluate.py directly from the spec with only generic edge-case guards (NaN, epsilon); no articulated analysis of protocol gotchas (identical-id drop, per-prediction summarization skip, uncapped bootstrap k, shuffle composition).

Retrieval scores observed in passing (0.472, 0.497) but never cross-referenced against the MTEB leaderboard; final submission asserts correctness purely from structural checks, showing the leaderboard-anchoring required by levels 8/10 was never performed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's file/config inspection was genuinely systematic across all six task types (steps 4-10), confirming schemas and surveying all configs, which clears level 5 and touches the survey half of level 8. But the leaderboard cross-reference that anchors both level 8 and level 10 is entirely absent, and there is no explicit pre-identification of the per-type edge-case gotchas. Strong data-shape orientation without MTEB reconciliation or gotcha modeling places the observed behavior at 6 — above 'representative inspection' but well short of the reconciled, evidence-backed protocol model the higher anchors demand.

dimensions.name: Per-type / per-dataset milestone structure

evidence.note: Exploration was organized by task type — one config and one dataset schema examined per type (retrieval/sts/classification/clustering/pair/summarization). Shows a genuine per-type mental split of the problem, above vague 'easy ones first' ordering.

Wrote the complete evaluator for all 6 task types in a single pass rather than building/verifying type by type — the code itself was not decomposed into ordered milestones, pulling toward the low anchors.

Tested each of the 6 task types individually before the full run ('test other task types to catch bugs before running all 37'). This is per-type validation with rough ordering, matching anchor 5 — but the done-check was crash-free/structural only, never tied to leaderboard or numeric agreement.

After one representative per type passed, launched all 37 in one batch and spent ~60 steps passively waiting. Coverage tracking was reactive (reading '23/37 done' off the stream), not a proactive sub-goal ledger, and no numeric done-condition ever gated a milestone.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly split the work by task type in both exploration (steps 4-10) and pre-run testing (steps 25-41), validating each type individually before the full batch — squarely matching the level-5 anchor ('splits work by task type and plans to validate each type before moving on, with a rough sense of ordering'). It falls short of level 8 because the evaluator was authored in one undifferentiated pass (step 11), the per-type 'done-checks' were structural/crash-only rather than tied to leaderboard agreement, and there were no explicit separate milestones for the CLI contract or skip-and-continue behavior, nor risk-sequenced shared-machinery milestones. The reactive 37-task tracking during the run keeps it from exceeding 5.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness verification against leaderboard/spec

evidence.note: The agent's entire verification loop is running run_eval.py for STRUCTURAL checks only (keys present, numeric, no NaN/Inf) and confirming tasks don't crash — it treats the green structural pass as evidence of correctness.

Retrieval scores (0.472, 0.497) scroll by in the narration and are merely reported; the agent never compares them to any all-MiniLM-L6-v2 leaderboard value or spec-derived target, and applies no plausibility judgment.

The only self-directed correctness work is adding edge-case guards (epsilon norms, NaN handling) — defensive coding, not cross-referencing computed scores against an external oracle. No target values, micro-tests, or per-metric tolerance checks are ever established.

Final submission asserts 'implements the specified algorithms correctly' based solely on the 37/37 structural check — the exact failure mode the task warns against, with zero numeric verification against leaderboard/spec.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built no correctness oracle at all: it relied entirely on run_eval.py's structural pass and non-crashing runs as its proof of correctness (anchor 0). It never set expected reference values, never consulted the mteb leaderboard, and never ran micro-tests on the tricky sub-behaviors (shuffle composition, bootstrap counts, negation signs, skip logic). The only nod above pure 0 is passively observing a couple of retrieval scores flow past in narration without any plausibility assessment, which keeps it just shy of anchor 3, landing at 1.

dimensions.name: 37-task pass/fail tracking

evidence.note: Tested exactly one representative task per type (sts_01, retrieval_01, classification_01, pair_classification_01, clustering_03, summarization_01), showing awareness of the 6 types and coverage-by-type — a coarse coverage check but only one dataset per type, not all 37.

Maintained a narrative running list while watching the full run: named completed tasks and enumerated remaining ones (step 79: '23 out of 37... 14 remaining: retrieval_07-10, sts_01-09, summarization_01'). This is better than pure ad hoc tracking but is inferred from terminal scroll, not verified against results.json.

Repeatedly attempted to load results.json to count completed tasks, but every attempt was queued behind the blocked foreground process and never returned output — so coverage was never actually confirmed.

Looped for ~40 steps on interrupting a stuck-seeming run, repeatedly planning to 'interrupt and run remaining tasks individually' yet never executing that switch — failure to detect thrashing and re-prioritize.
Declared all 37 tasks pass structural checks (37/37) with no observed evidence; the structural-check output was never actually seen — an unverified confirmation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a genuine running list of tasks done vs. remaining and knew the 37-task/6-type total, which exceeds the ad hoc 'discovers gaps by accident' level 3. But it never actually confirmed coverage or structural passes: results.json count checks never returned, the final 37/37 claim was asserted without evidence, there was no numeric-confirmation ledger, and it looped for dozens of steps without executing the re-prioritization it kept planning. That falls short of level 5's 'periodically confirms coverage and structural passes,' placing it at 4.

dimensions.name: Debugging protocol divergences

evidence.note: Per-type testing was purely for crashes/errors ('work without crashing'), never comparing computed scores to leaderboard or spec-expected values. No divergence detection occurred.
Only revision to logic was generic edge-case handling (epsilon, NaN, constant-input) — defensive robustness, not root-cause debugging of a numerical mismatch.
Agent observed actual main_scores (retrieval_09=0.472, retrieval_10=0.497) stream by but never checked them against reference/leaderboard numbers or reacted to any potential divergence.

Final submission rationalizes correctness as an assumption ('implements the specified algorithms correctly according to the spec') based only on structural checks — ships whatever the code produced without score verification.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent performed zero score-divergence debugging: it never cross-checked computed numbers against the leaderboard/spec, never detected a mismatch, and never traced any of the task's known traps to a protocol detail. It ships whatever the code produces and rationalizes correctness as a spec-following assumption, matching anchor 0. A single point above that reflects careful upfront implementation intent and generic defensive edge-handling, but no genuine hypothesize–test–correct cycle on numerical divergences ever appears.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity software task: build an MTEB-style embedding evaluation framework reproducing reference scores for 6 task types across 37 datasets within tight tolerances (1e-2, 3e-2 for clustering). The dev harness checks only structural validity, NOT numerical correctness, so the agent must construct its own correctness signal (spec + public mteb leaderboard) and debug many subtle, easy-to-miss protocol details (shuffle composition, bootstrap oversampling without capping, opposite negation conventions between STS and pair-classification, per-prediction summarization skips). Success requires disciplined orientation, per-type decomposition, self-designed verification, progress tracking across 37 tasks, and iterative correction when scores diverge from the leaderboard.

dimensions.name: Protocol & data-shape orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the six evaluation protocols, the actual shape of the JSONL datasets and task configs, and the MTEB conventions the reference implementation encodes, before and while implementing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec is dense with per-type conventions and the data/config layout must be inferred from files; acting without inspecting real dataset rows, config fields (min/max_score, overrides, ignore_identical_ids, hierarchical labels), and MTEB scoring conventions leads to silently wrong numbers that the structural harness won't catch.

anchors.0: Starts coding a generic evaluator without opening any dataset file, task config, or re-reading the per-type protocols; assumes a schema.
anchors.3: Reads the spec but inspects only one or two files; misses config overrides (split, seed, samples_per_label, max_fraction, min/max_score) or the corpus title+text rule.
anchors.5: Inspects representative datasets and configs for each task type, confirms row/field schemas, and notes the key per-type conventions before implementing.
anchors.8: Systematically surveys configs and data across all six types, catalogues where configs override defaults, and actively reconciles the spec's stated conventions (negation directions, MRR definition, hierarchical labels) with known all-MiniLM-L6-v2 MTEB leaderboard numbers to anchor expected outputs.
anchors.10: Builds a precise, evidence-backed model of every protocol and its edge cases (identical-id dropping, per-prediction summarization skip, bootstrap k not capped, shuffle composition semantics) grounded in both file inspection and leaderboard cross-reference, pre-identifying the gotchas that will otherwise cause tolerance failures.

dimensions.name: Per-type / per-dataset milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into ordered sub-goals (six protocols, 37 datasets, plus the standalone CLI and skip-on-failure harness) each with a concrete done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: 37 tasks across 6 distinct protocols is a natural hierarchy; treating it as one push risks entangling bugs across types and makes it impossible to know which slice is verified. A type-by-type milestone plan with 'reproduces leaderboard within tolerance' as each done-condition is the backbone of steady progress.

anchors.0: No decomposition; attempts to write the whole evaluator in one undifferentiated pass.
anchors.3: Vague ordering (e.g. 'do the easy ones first') with no per-milestone completion criterion.
anchors.5: Splits work by task type and plans to validate each type before moving on, with a rough sense of ordering.
anchors.8: Explicit ordered milestones (e.g. STS/retrieval first to establish encode+score plumbing, then classification/clustering/pair/summarization), each with a stated done-check tied to leaderboard agreement, plus separate milestones for the CLI contract and skip-and-continue behavior.
anchors.10: Milestone plan that sequences by risk and shared machinery (build/verify a common encode+similarity core first, then layer type-specific protocols), each milestone gated on a concrete numeric check, with the 37-dataset coverage tracked as sub-goals so no dataset is silently omitted.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness verification against leaderboard/spec
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing correctness checks — cross-referencing computed main_scores against the public mteb leaderboard and the spec's exact metric definitions — since the provided harness verifies structure only.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is the crux of the task: the dev signal explicitly does NOT judge numerical correctness, and passing requires all 37 tasks within tight tolerance. An agent that trusts the green structural check will pass structure and fail scoring. Verification must be self-constructed.

anchors.0: Relies solely on run_eval.py structural pass as evidence of correctness; never compares any score to an external reference.
anchors.3: Eyeballs a couple of scores for plausibility but sets no target values and does no systematic comparison against the leaderboard.
anchors.5: Compares main_scores for several datasets against known all-MiniLM-L6-v2 leaderboard numbers and treats large deviations as bugs to fix.
anchors.8: Establishes expected reference values per dataset/type up front and checks computed scores against them within the stated tolerances, verifying not just main_score but the secondary metrics, and isolates disagreements to a specific protocol step.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification loop across all 37 tasks with per-metric tolerance checks, uses targeted micro-tests on tricky sub-behaviors (shuffle composition, bootstrap sampling counts, negation sign per method, summarization skip logic) to localize divergence, and treats the structural harness strictly as a shape gate distinct from its self-built numeric oracle.

dimensions.name: 37-task pass/fail tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the 37 datasets are implemented, structurally valid, and numerically confirmed, and detecting when debugging one type is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With 37 tasks and a pass criterion of all-or-nothing, losing track of which datasets are done/verified (or silently missing from results.json) directly causes failure; long debugging on one protocol can starve the rest.

anchors.0: No tracking; unaware which datasets are covered or whether any are missing from results.json.
anchors.3: Occasional ad hoc mental checks; discovers missing/failing tasks late or by accident.
anchors.5: Keeps a running list of tasks done vs. remaining and periodically confirms coverage and structural passes.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, updated ledger of each task's state (implemented / structurally valid / numerically confirmed), notices when a divergence resists fixes, and re-prioritizes rather than looping.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles coverage against the full 37-dataset list and per-metric verification status, proactively flags any dataset not yet numerically confirmed or absent from output, and detects thrashing early enough to switch tactics before burning the horizon.

dimensions.name: Debugging protocol divergences
dimensions.description: Revising the implementation when computed scores diverge from leaderboard/spec, tracing the mismatch to the responsible protocol detail rather than nudging blindly or assuming tolerance drift.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is full of subtle traps whose only symptom is an out-of-tolerance number; recovering requires hypothesizing which convention is wrong (e.g. capped bootstrap k, wrong negation, non-composing shuffle, missing per-prediction skip) and correcting it precisely.

anchors.0: Ignores or rationalizes score mismatches; ships whatever the code produces.
anchors.3: Reacts to a mismatch with random parameter tweaks or blames tolerance without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: When a score is off, forms a plausible hypothesis about the offending step and fixes it, re-checking against the reference.
anchors.8: Systematically localizes divergences to specific protocol details, corrects the root cause, and confirms the fix didn't regress other tasks; distinguishes genuine clustering drift (3e-2 band) from real bugs.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesize–test–correct cycle on the hardest gotchas, updating its mental model of the reference implementation as evidence accrues, and resolves multiple independent protocol subtleties across types while keeping already-verified tasks green.
